Aristotle revisits the nature of unity and being, having closed his discussion of mathematical objects. Unity and being are coextensive: whatever is, is one. But "one" admits of many senses, as does "being"—they are said analogically. Aquinas deeply approves this analogical approach, for it resolves the apparent paradox that being is both utterly simple (a fundamental transcendental convertible with unity itself) and infinitely diverse (appearing in infinite forms in creation). God is pure being, absolutely simple, purely one. All creatures have being by participation; in each, act and potentiality are distinct, so unity is achieved through form imposing order on matter. Unity in creatures is therefore never absolute or unqualified, but always qualified by the degree of actualization and the composition present. This chapter sets the stage for a metaphysical re-examination of how unity and being relate in the caused realm, reaffirming that the analogy of being is the master-key to all philosophical understanding.

The discussion turns to the distinction between unity-as-continuity (in substances, especially bodies) and unity-as-identity (in concepts and universals). A human being is one through the continuous unity of matter and form, through the actual integration of potentialities into a single substantial form. Yet the concept "human" is also one—the universal shared by many particulars. Aquinas sees both as real: the unity of the substance is a unity-in-act (unum secundum actum), grounded in the substantial form; the unity of the universal is a unity-of-concept (unum in ratione), which is "one" as an object of intellection but exists in many (vel in multis, according to the maxim). The metaphysical mystery deepens: how can the one universal truly be in many? Through the act-potency structure: the nature (human-ness) is potential to instantiation in many particulars; it is actualized variously in each. This chapter crystallizes the medieval recovery of Aristotelian realism against both nominalist dissolution and Platonic reification of universals.

Aristotle addresses the unity of substance versus the unity of the universal, pushing harder. Is the principle of unity in a substance (this man) the same as the principle of unity in the concept "man"? No, replies Aristotle (with Aquinas in full accord). In the individual substance, unity comes from the substantial form that actualizes prime matter and integrates all accidents into a single being. In the universal, unity comes from the intellect's grasping of a common nature. Both unities are real, but their grounds are different. This distinction is vital to Aquinas's entire metaphysics: it prevents the confusion of the transcendental order (where being and unity reign) with the conceptual order (where universals reside). A failure to distinguish leads either to nominalism (denying real universals) or to Platonism (making universals into separate substances). The via media of Aristotelian-Thomistic realism holds fast: real essences in things, abstracted by intellect into universal concepts, both genuinely real at their respective levels.

The question of numerical identity becomes acute. Is the universal "Socrates" (his individual nature considered as a principle of his properties) the same as "Socrates" (the concrete existent individual)? In one sense yes: they are identified in reality. In another sense no: the universal is considered apart from particularity, while the existent is singular. Aquinas's doctrine of the compositionality of creature-being resolves this: Socrates is a composite of essence and existence (essentia et existentia). His essence—what makes him human, his humanity—is a universal principle (capable, in itself, of being in multiple instances). But this essence is *this* essence, actualized in *this* existent by a unique act of being (actus essendi). Thus identity and distinction cohere: Socrates's individual being is the actualization of a unique universal essence, united uniquely to an act-of-being that is his alone. This intricate metaphysics explains how the eternal Forms of Plato are unnecessary; God, knowing all essences eternally in His infinite intellect, creates a universe of singular instances, each a unique hypostasis of an intelligible nature.

Aristotle explores whether contrariety and opposition illuminate the nature of being and unity. Contraries (hot/cold, large/small) are linked by a common genus or subject; they are not simple opposites but opposites *within* a field of potentiality. Aquinas recognizes here the profound insight that being-and-not-being, act-and-potency, are not brute opposites. Rather, potency is a real principle, a "not-yet-actualized" capacity oriented toward act. Contraries in the sensible world reflect this fundamental structure: they arise in a common subject (a body can be hot or cold) and represent different actualizations of a shared potentiality. Contrariety thus bespeaks the metaphysical composition of all creatures: they are potentiality seeking actualization through form. Even at the level of being itself, an analysis of contrariety illuminates how creation is neither absolute non-being (which cannot have contraries) nor the infinite undifferentiated being of the divine nature (which knows no contrariety), but a realm of participative being where multiplicity and change are grounded in act-potency. This chapter shows why opposition, properly understood, reveals the metaphysical structure of all that-is-not-God.

Aristotle concludes by affirming that the science of being-qua-being (metaphysics) has analyzed the deepest structures of all that exists. Unity, being, substance, cause, act-potency—these form the irreducible framework in which all intelligibility resides. For Aquinas, this represents philosophy's highest achievement: to articulate the conceptual architecture of reality itself, showing how all things flow from the absolutely simple, self-subsisting being of God, and how all created being exhibits the fundamental structure of composition, dependence, and participation. The entire Metaphysics culminates here: from the wonder at sensible things that sparked inquiry (Book I), through the systematic analysis of causation, substance, and form, to the recognition that all coherence, unity, and intelligibility derive from the transcendent One. Metaphysics thus becomes a philosophical hymn to the Creator, even if Aristotle himself did not name Him as such. For Christian Aquinas, this Aristotelian metaphysics provides the rational foundation upon which revealed theology—the knowledge of God in His inner life, His creation, His redemption—can be erected without contradiction, fulfilling the truth that faith seeks understanding.
